newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's Ahern casts himself as man of people.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Ahern casts himself as man of people.

text.p: Bertie Ahern has cast himself as a man of the people in a month-long election campaign that has taken him to the high Street of every village and town in Ireland.
He has kissed babies, belles and grandmothers, stopping only to assail Prime Minister John Bruton's government for failing to crack down on crime, public spending and unemployment.
Ahern, the 45-year-old leader of the centre-right Fianna Fail party, is bidding to end Bruton's two-and-a-half years in power when Ireland's two million voters go to the polls on Friday.
Groomed from his earliest days by the barons who control Fianna Fail, Ireland's biggest and most potent political party, Ahern was robbed of the leadership of the nation in 1994.
That was when the then leader of the party, former prime minister Albert Reynolds, stepped down in a row with its junior coalition partner, the Labour party, over legal appointments.
Labour switched its support to Bruton's Fine Gael which formed an untested alliance which included the radical Democratic Left grouping, and Ahern was forced to wait.
Friends say the spell in opposition has helped him get to grips with party machinery, and smoothe the edges of a fairly raw personal image.

Ahern's political handlers have cast him as the voice of modern Ireland, a rapidly developing and prosperous state but one which is proud of its traditions and past and cherishes its uniqueness in what it sees as a homogenising Europe.
It is a tactic designed to capture the imagination of the small rural farmer and the Dublin housewife, the village shopkeeper and the city computer professional.
A devout but pragmatic Catholic, a young but experienced politician, Ahern has promised something for everyone in a campaign run under the slogan: "People before politics."
He has pledged that the people of Ireland would enjoy the fruits of an unprecedented economic boom by bringing down the top rate of tax from 48 percent to 45 over the next five years.

At the same time he has also said that the search for a Northern Ireland settlement would be the top priority of a government led by the party which sees itself as the Irish Republican party, committed to regaining control of the British province.

Despite his relative youth, Ahern is a vastly experienced politician having served as labour minister, finance minister and even mayor of Dublin in a political career that began in 1977 when he was first elected to parliament.
Economic analysts have commended his handling of Ireland's devaluation crisis in January 1993, since when the economy, partly due to outside factors, has fared well.
Ahern is seen in the party as a protege of Charles Haughey, who was prime minister three times.
"He shares with his political mentor Charles Haughey a certain elusive charm and is comfortable with his man of the people image," one profiler said of the avid sports fan.

But Ahern quickly distanced himself from Haughey when a payments to politicians tribunal shortly before the election was told that the ex-premier had been given more than a million pounds by tycoon Ben Dunne for unspecified purposes.

He also, friends say, has done something about his dress sense. He was dubbed "anorak man" in his early days for his choice of casual sports attire but the double-breasted suit and artfully knotted tie have replaced all that.

Born in 1951 in the city's Northside suburb of Drumcondra, he still lives there and has a powerful grass-roots party following and fund-raising machine in the city. He studied at Dublin's University College and the London School of Economics.

A Catholic who is conservative on social issues such as abortion, contraception and divorce, he nevertheless separated from his wife of 19 years, Miriam Kelly, blaming the stress of his job. But he still sees a lot of his two teenage daughters.
His public discussion of his marriage and his admission that he has a girlfriend is unusual for Irish politicians and a separated prime minister would be unprecedented.
"He is every great Irish mother's son," the Irish Times said in 1993. "He may not wear odd socks but his oversized suits, slight stutter and constant gulping have endeared him to the public."
